item.title: When Waiting Becomes Part of Illness
item.description:
Anxiety

When Waiting Becomes Part of Illness

Reframing waiting through the lens of psychologically informed healthcare.

Posted July 17, 2026

Key points
  • Waiting is a healthcare experience that shapes well-being, trust, and recovery.
  • Lack of information encourages fear, worry, and worst-case thinking.
  • Families and caregivers experience uncertainty and emotional strain too.
  • Compassionate communication can significantly reduce the burden of waiting.

Imagine being told there may be something seriously wrong with you or your child, only to learn that you must wait weeks or months for answers. Within healthcare systems, waiting is often treated as a logistical problem. For patients and caregivers, it can be deeply distressing. The psychological burden of illness does not begin with diagnosis or treatment. For many people, it begins with the wait for both.

One of the Hardest Parts of Living with a Chronic Illness Is the Waiting

As a psychologist and lifelong congenital heart patient, I have spent much of my life waiting. From infancy, I have spent countless hours waiting by the phone for doctors to call, in outpatient clinics for appointments, in accident and emergency care, and for the results of tests, procedures, and surgeries. During hospital admissions, I have to wait for my slot on the surgical list, for cannulas and stitches to be removed, for pain relief, for discharge letters, and for permission to finally go home. Much of that waiting occurs when I am frightened, unwell, vulnerable, and uncertain about what might happen next. Even as a young child, for some healthcare procedures and surgeries, I had to wait without the soothing presence of loved ones. From a psychological perspective, waiting can be profoundly threatening.

The Nervous System Doesn't Wait Calmly

People can often cope remarkably well with difficult news. What is typically much harder is uncertainty. Our brains are prediction machines, constantly scanning the environment for signs of safety or threat. When information is incomplete, the mind naturally attempts to fill in the gaps. What if the test result is bad? What if my condition is getting worse? What if they have forgotten about me? What if the surgery goes wrong?

Living in this state of chronic anticipation can activate the body's threat response. The brain’s hypothalamus triggers a "fight-or-flight" response, prompting the adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol. While these hormones are vital for immediate safety, chronic activation of this system by ongoing stressors can cause long-term health issues.

Uncertainty becomes a danger signal, triggering hypervigilance, worry, sleep disturbance, difficulty concentrating, and emotional distress. In short, we no longer feel psychologically safe. As many patients know, some of the hardest moments occur not during treatment itself, but while waiting to find out what their treatment will be.

When Time Allows Fear to Grow

Waiting gives you time to think. Impotent, time allows fear to grow. Without information, the mind often fills the gaps with imagined possibilities. For some, this may involve catastrophic scenarios. For others, it manifests as pacing around the house, repeatedly checking symptoms, endlessly searching online, or jumping every time the phone rings.

Not only do you need to manage any ongoing symptoms and physical limitations, but the impact of waiting ripples throughout life. You may postpone social plans in case a healthcare professional calls. You may struggle to focus on work or need to take extended time off on sick leave. You find yourself becoming more irritable, distracted, and emotionally exhausted. You wonder whether to contact your healthcare provider again, while worrying about being perceived as demanding or labelled a "difficult patient." Major life decisions are often put on hold, the future feels suspended. Elevated stress can disrupt sleep, increase fatigue, create muscle tension, affect digestion, intensify symptom monitoring, and undermine mood and daily functioning.

Why Waiting Feels Like Powerlessness

One reason waiting is so difficult is that it often involves a profound loss of control. This loss of agency can heighten feelings of vulnerability and helplessness. Research consistently links powerlessness with increased anxiety, depression, trauma-related distress, and poorer psychological well-being. Patients frequently describe feeling invisible, forgotten, or unimportant, understandable human responses to uncertainty and loss of control.

When we feel vulnerable, we naturally seek reassurance and safety from others. A delayed appointment, unanswered voicemail, or missed call back may seem minor from an organisational perspective. Yet as a patient, it can carry a powerful emotional message. Compassionate communication, therefore, is not simply administration; it is the cornerstone of healthcare.

The emotional burden often extends across entire families. Throughout my own healthcare journey, parents, partners, children, and friends have waited alongside me. They too have lived with uncertainty, fear, and helplessness. For loved ones, there is often little they can do except wait and worry.

When Waiting Reawakens Old Wounds

Not everyone experiences waiting in the same way. Waiting can be particularly difficult for people with previous medical trauma, adverse childhood experiences, health anxiety, or histories of neglect, abandonment, or loss. For these individuals, a delayed phone call, postponed appointment, or delay in outpatient care may represent more than an administrative inconvenience. It can reactivate deeply held fears about safety, vulnerability, and whether support will be available when needed.

Understanding this can help healthcare professionals appreciate why seemingly small delays can evoke powerful emotional reactions and why training in responding compassionately is essential at every touch point.

A Psychologically Informed Approach to Waiting

The good news is that reducing the psychological burden of waiting does not always require vast resources. Consistent with a psychologically informed approach to healthcare, relatively small changes can make a meaningful difference:

  • Explain what happens next, keep patients informed about delays, and offer realistic timelines.
  • Provide a clear point of contact and maintain contact during prolonged waits.
  • Communicate clearly with compassion at every stage of care.
  • Avoid unnecessary secondary waiting lists and administrative hurdles.
  • Acknowledge emotional distress and take into account the patient's history and any medical trauma.
  • Value patients' time as a healthcare outcome in its own right.
  • Allow a loved one to wait with patients.

For patients:

  • Know your patient rights and be polite but assertive.
  • Use an advocate, trusted friend, or a chaperone.
  • Keep a record of healthcare interactions, noting appointment dates, phone calls, names of professionals, advice given, and next steps.
  • Become an informed expert by learning about your condition and keep a concise summary of your health information, including key contact details, diagnosis and medications.
  • Look after your well-being while you wait.
  • Avoid excessive symptom-checking and internet searching.
  • Seek support if waiting is affecting your mental health, from family, friends, peer support organisations, or professionals.

Psychologically informed healthcare requires us to recognise waiting as a significant healthcare experience rather than just empty time between clinical events. Across the healthcare journey, how patients experience waiting can profoundly shape well-being, recovery, trust, engagement with services, and future help-seeking behaviour. For many patients, the most difficult part of illness is not what happens in the consultation room. It is what happens while they wait outside it.

Adapted from Morton, L (2025). Beyond the Medical Gaze: Practicing Psychologically Informed Healthcare, Oxford University Press.

item.title: When Grief Changes How We See the World
item.description:
Grief

When Grief Changes How We See the World

How personal loss changed the way I listened to other people's stories.

Posted July 17, 2026

Key points
  • Personal loss can change how we understand another person's experience.
  • Grief often appears during ordinary moments rather than major life events.
  • Listening to another person's story can deepen our understanding of our own loss.
  • Continuing bonds help explain why loved ones remain part of our lives after death.
Source: pexels-brett-sayles

Shortly after my mother died, I participated in a restorative justice circle. I have attended many circles over the years as part of my work in forensic psychology, and each one has reminded me that every person carries a story that is often invisible to others. Participants come together to talk about experiences that have affected their lives while everyone else listens with respect and without interruption. I arrived expecting to hear another meaningful discussion. I did not expect the experience to affect me personally.

One of the participants was a young man whom I will call Camilo to protect his privacy. When it was his turn to speak, he took a deep breath and said he wanted to talk about his mother. He described how difficult life had become after she died. He spoke about reaching for his phone because he wanted to call her, only to remember that she was no longer there. He talked about family gatherings that no longer felt the same and about moments when her absence became impossible to ignore.

As I listened, I realized that I was hearing his story differently than I would have only a few months earlier.

For most of my professional life, I have listened to people describe painful experiences. I have heard stories about violence, abuse, trauma, and loss. My training helped me understand how those experiences affect thoughts, emotions, and behavior. That afternoon, however, I found myself responding in a way that was new to me. I was not only listening as a psychologist. I was also listening as a son who had recently lost his mother.

When Another Person's Story Feels Familiar

Camilo's experience was not the same as mine. Our families were different, and the circumstances surrounding our losses were different. Even so, there were moments during his story that felt familiar. I understood what he meant when he described returning home and expecting, for just a second, that his mother would still be there. I understood why ordinary moments had become the hardest ones.

Before my mother's death, I believed I had a good understanding of grief. I had worked with grieving families, read the research, and taught students about bereavement. Looking back, I realize that knowledge gave me an understanding of grief as a psychological process. Living through the loss of my own mother gave me a different understanding. It became personal.

That realization stayed with me throughout the rest of the restorative justice circle. I was no longer thinking only about the psychological meaning of Camilo's words. I was thinking about my own mother and about the many small ways her absence had become part of my daily life.

Listening Changed

After my mother's death, I noticed changes that I had not expected. I paid closer attention when someone spoke about losing a parent. I found myself remembering conversations long after they ended. Sometimes a single sentence remained with me for days because it reminded me of something I had experienced myself.

Research over the past few years has shown that many bereaved individuals continue an inner relationship with the person who died. Rather than viewing this connection as a sign that someone has failed to adjust, researchers increasingly recognize that these continuing bonds often become part of healthy adaptation to loss (Hewson et al., 2024). Reading those findings helped me understand something I had already begun to experience. My mother's influence had not ended with her death. She remained present in my memories, in the values she taught me, and in the way I now listened to other people.

Camilo helped me recognize that change. He never intended to do that. He was simply telling his story.

Ordinary Moments Carry New Meaning

People often associate grief with anniversaries, funerals, or birthdays. My experience has been different. Many of the moments that remind me of my mother happen without warning. They appear during an ordinary day while talking to someone, hearing a familiar expression, or remembering something she once said.

Researchers have also found that these continuing bonds often become part of the way people rebuild meaning after losing someone they love. The relationship changes over time, but it does not disappear. Many people continue to feel connected through memories, shared values, family traditions, and everyday decisions (Black et al., 2022).

As I reflected on Camilo's story, I realized that grief had changed more than my personal life. It had changed the way I connected with the experiences of others. I still listened carefully, just as I always had, but my understanding now included something that no textbook could have taught me.

A Circle That Stayed With Me

When the restorative justice circle ended, people slowly left the room. I remained seated for a few minutes, thinking about everything I had heard. I came to the circle expecting to learn about someone else's experience. Instead, I left with a deeper understanding of my own.

Losing my mother has been one of the most difficult experiences of my life. Like many people, I continue to miss her in ways that are difficult to predict. Some days I think about her because of an important family event. Other days, I remember her because of something as simple as a conversation.

I still remember Camilo's story. I remember the silence in the room while everyone listened. I remember realizing that grief had changed the way I heard his words. That afternoon reminded me that every person enters a conversation carrying experiences that others cannot always see. Sometimes we recognize a part of ourselves in another person's story. Sometimes that recognition helps us understand our own lives a little better.

item.title: Is Psychology Ignoring One of the Biggest Human Mysteries?
item.description:
Psychology

Is Psychology Ignoring One of the Biggest Human Mysteries?

The human story behind UAP deserves the attention of psychological science.

Posted July 17, 2026

Key points
  • Every aspect of the UAP story involves the psychology of the human mind.
  • Psychologists are not immune to the very psychological issues they study.
  • Psychologists have both a scientific opportunity and an ethical responsibility to engage on the topic of UAPs.
Source: AI-Generated / Open AI

For more than a century, the field of psychology has sought to understand human thought, emotion, perception, belief, memory, and behavior. It has tackled some of humanity’s most complex questions, from consciousness and trauma to religion, spirituality, and extraordinary human experiences. Yet there is one area where, despite millions of reported experiences and increasing attention from governments and scientists, the field has remained remarkably quiet: unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP).

Whether UAPs ultimately prove to represent misunderstood natural phenomena, advanced technology, non-human intelligence, or something else entirely is a question for many scientific disciplines to investigate. But there is another question that belongs squarely within the expertise of psychologists: What can these experiences teach us about the human mind?

Over the past several years, the conversation surrounding UAP has changed dramatically. Senior government officials, military personnel, intelligence officers, scientists, and members of Congress have publicly stated that some UAP reports cannot currently be explained by known technologies or conventional explanations. Governments around the world have expanded efforts to collect and analyze data. Regardless of where these investigations ultimately lead, the topic has moved well beyond the realm of popular culture.

Yet the field of psychology has largely remained on the sidelines.

That absence is difficult to understand.

If millions of people across cultures and throughout history report extraordinary experiences, psychologists should be interested. If those experiences influence people’s beliefs, identities, relationships, and mental health, psychologists should be interested. If the possibility of future disclosure has the potential to shape how individuals and societies think, feel, and adapt, psychologists should certainly be interested.

At the same time, if these reports prove to have conventional explanations, we would still be left with one of the most remarkable psychological questions of our time. How do millions of people, across different cultures and generations, come to report experiences that share striking similarities? What roles do perception, memory, expectation, belief, social influence, culture, or consciousness play? Understanding that phenomenon would itself represent a major scientific contribution.

Either possibility deserves serious investigation.

The field of psychology has never required certainty before asking important questions. Psychologists study uncertainty itself. We investigate perception without fully understanding consciousness, memory despite its imperfections, and human behavior despite its extraordinary complexity. Our responsibility is not to wait until every mystery has been solved. It is to better understand the human experience.

So why has the field of psychology remained largely absent? Part of the answer, I believe, is institutional stigma.

For decades, UAP has been associated with ridicule, sensationalism, and reputational risk. Researchers who expressed interest in the topic often found themselves defending the legitimacy of the subject before anyone evaluated the quality of their work. Over time, this stigma shaped funding decisions, publication opportunities, academic careers, and ultimately the willingness of many scientists to engage with the topic at all.

The field of psychology is not separate from the psychologists who comprise it. Like every scientific discipline, it is shaped by the questions we choose to ask, the topics we pursue, the research we fund, the papers we publish, and the conversations we are willing to have. When an important area of human experience receives little scientific attention, it is worth asking not only what we may have overlooked, but why.

Ironically, psychologists have spent decades studying the very processes that may have contributed to this silence.

Psychologists understand that stigma discourages disclosure, influences perception, alters behavior, and limits inquiry. We recognize that social pressures can determine which experiences people are willing to report and which questions researchers feel comfortable pursuing. We routinely study conformity, group norms, reputational concerns, and institutional influences on decision-making. It would be surprising if the field of psychology itself were somehow immune to these same psychological processes.

Recognizing the influence of stigma does not require abandoning scientific skepticism. In fact, it demands the opposite. Genuine neutral skepticism asks difficult questions, follows evidence wherever it leads, and resists allowing social pressures to determine which scientific questions deserve attention. The goal is not to validate extraordinary claims. The goal is to investigate extraordinary human experiences with rigor, intellectual humility, and methodological excellence.

The field of psychology has a unique contribution to make. Psychologists are uniquely qualified to investigate perception, cognition, memory, belief formation, identity, uncertainty, resilience, adaptation, and the psychological effects of worldview-changing information. If consciousness plays any role in how these experiences occur or are interpreted, psychologists should be among the scientists helping to investigate that possibility. If consciousness plays no role, psychologists are still essential to understanding how people perceive, interpret, remember, and integrate extraordinary experiences into their lives.

These questions matter regardless of what UAPs actually are.

This topic is about much more than just understanding UAP, it is about the future of the field of psychology. Scientific progress depends on our willingness to examine our own assumptions, confront institutional stigma, and ask difficult questions with curiosity and humility. If this phenomenon has the potential to deepen our understanding of perception, consciousness, belief, and human adaptation, then the field of psychology has both a scientific opportunity and an ethical responsibility to help investigate it.

item.title: Why Fearing Failure Makes It More Likely
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Why Fearing Failure Makes It More Likely

Fear can make us change the goal, narrow our options, or cede the initiative.

Posted July 17, 2026

Key points
  • Once people have something to lose, they sometimes stop pursuing success and start protecting what they have.
  • Stress can make an old solution feel safer, even when the situation has changed.
  • A defensive move can reduce risk but still leave opponents free to set the terms.
  • Ask what winning requires now, what has changed, and who is setting the terms.

England went 1–0 ahead against Argentina in the 55th minute of their 2026 World Cup semi-final, then became increasingly passive. In the 72nd minute, manager Thomas Tuchel replaced goalscorer Anthony Gordon with defender Ezri Konsa and moved to a back five.

By the time Lautaro Martínez completed Argentina’s comeback 38 minutes after England’s goal, England had managed only 12 percent possession. By then, England’s defeat had begun to feel increasingly likely. Messi went on to create both late goals, sending Argentina through to the final.

We cannot know what motivated Tuchel. But the pattern is familiar. Once people have something to lose, they often stop asking what success requires and start protecting what they already have.

Why does this happen, and what can we do to resist it?

Fear of failure does not merely make us anxious about achieving our goal. It can quietly replace the goal itself. It moves our focus from winning to avoiding defeat, from initiating to reacting, and from facing the present to repeating the past.

1. Fear Changes the Goal

Psychologists distinguish between approach goals, focused on achieving a positive result, and avoidance goals, focused on preventing a negative one. Approach goals are generally associated with better performance, and fear of failure with greater reliance on performance-avoidance goals.

Before England scored, the team was trying to win. Afterward, they played increasingly as though protecting the lead mattered more than extending it.

To resist such shifts, reset the goal. Ask: What would I do now if I had no lead to protect? Admittedly, this is easier said than done when you’re under pressure and the stakes are high. But it’s precisely what’s needed to restore the original objective before fear moves the goalposts.

2. Fear Narrows the Repertoire

Under threat, people narrow their attention and fall back on familiar responses, a pattern known as threat rigidity.

England’s retreat into a back five against Mexico in an earlier round of the competition had been hailed as a tactical masterclass. But the circumstances were very different. England were down to 10 men, playing the co-hosts on their home turf, and protecting a 3–2 lead. They also retained an outlet for counterattacks. Against Argentina, the same structure left them with little capacity to relieve pressure and gave Messi repeated opportunities to take control of the match.

I’ve been there too. In an undergraduate philosophy exam, I once panicked and reproduced much of an essay on Russell’s theory of descriptions that had earned me a First the previous year, even though the new question was asking something quite different. Suffice to say, the result did not get me into the philosophy world cup final.

So, before repeating a successful tactic, ask: What’s different this time? The question is not whether a tactic worked before. It’s whether it fits the situation now.

3. Fear Cedes the Initiative

The first two shifts have a strategic consequence. Once we focus on avoiding loss and retreat to familiar tactics, we are more likely to surrender the initiative and think less creatively.

England’s retreat not only reduced its own attacking threat but also allowed Argentina to determine where and how the rest of the match would be played. Similarly, leaders who become consumed by responding to critics, protecting past decisions, and preventing further losses allow opponents or circumstances to set the agenda.

So, even when retreat is necessary, preserve some capacity to shape what happens next. Ask: Who or what is setting the terms now? Then identify one move that requires others to respond to you.

The lesson is not that an attack is always the best form of defense. Sometimes defending is exactly what is required. The challenge is to distinguish tactical defense from psychological retreat.

When the stakes rise, familiarity can masquerade as wisdom and caution as control. Before falling back, ask the question that fear makes it hardest to face:

What’s required of me right now to succeed?
